title: Constant-rate binary locally decodable codes with logarithmic query complexity
formal: Do there exist constants \(r\in\)(0,1], \(\delta \in (0,1/2)\) and \(A>0\) such that, for arbitrarily large message lengths k, there are an integer n with \(k\le n\le k/r\), an encoding \(C:\{0,1\}^{k}\to \{0,1\}^{n}\), and randomized local decoders \(Dec_{i}\) for \(i\in \{1,\ldots ,k\}\), satisfying the following? For every message x, every received word \(z\in \{0,1\}^{n}\) differing from \(C(x)\) in fewer than \(\delta n\) positions, and every requested index \(i, Dec_{i}\) with oracle access to z outputs \(x_{i}\) with probability at least \(2/3\) while making at most \(\lceil A \log _{2}(n+1)\rceil\) bit queries on every execution.
why: A central locality-versus-redundancy barrier with consequences for private information retrieval and matrix rigidity.
status_note: The 2 April 2026 source explicitly identifies this binary problem as open. The January 2026 HDX result has different decoding guarantees. A search through 11 September 2026 found no resolution of the stated ordinary binary query model; this is a bounded literature check, not an independent proof audit.
review_note: Separated message and codeword lengths, bit queries and symbol queries, worst-case corruption and decoder randomness. Kept an information-theoretic existence target for unbounded lengths rather than adding efficient construction. Primary definition and open-question section read; related 2026 abstract checked.

progress.text: As summarized in the April 2026 source, constant-rate local decoding has an \(\Omega (\log  n)\) query lower bound and a binary high-rate upper bound of \(2^{O(\sqrt{\log  n\cdot \log  \log  n})}\).
HDX constructions improve approximate local list decoding and give logarithmic-depth list decoding, in a distinct model.
The revised large-alphabet LDC paper explicitly retains the ordinary binary constant-rate \(O(\log  n)\)-query question as open.

sentences: Can a binary code protect arbitrarily long messages at constant rate while recovering any requested bit with only logarithmically many bit queries?
A fixed positive fraction of the stored bits may be corrupted adversarially.
The local decoder must return the requested bit with probability at least two thirds for every admissible received word and index.
Large-alphabet and list-decoding results satisfy different guarantees.
The target asks for existence, without an extra requirement that the code be efficiently constructed.

upgraded_from.title: Constant-rate binary locally decodable codes with logarithmic query complexity

definitions: Here k counts message bits and n counts stored codeword bits; rate is \(k/n\) and Hamming distance counts unequal coordinates. “Arbitrarily large” means that every threshold K is exceeded by an admissible k; the constants \(r, \delta\) and A must be fixed before K. The encoding is deterministic and injective. A decoder knows C, k, n and the requested index, but learns the received word only by querying named coordinates, each returning one bit. Queries may be adaptive. A randomized decoder can be represented as a probability distribution over finite binary decision trees with the stated depth bound, whose leaves output 0 or 1. Computation, description length and encoding time are unrestricted: this is the source’s existence question, without an additional requirement of efficient uniform construction. The success guarantee is separate for each triple \((x,z,i)\); it does not require one random seed to recover all bits simultaneously. The adversary may choose corruptions knowing x and C, but z is fixed before the decoder’s private randomness. There is no secret key, channel-computation bound or input-dependent auxiliary information. The decoder must return the requested bit, rather than an erasure or a list of candidates.
answer_criterion: Prove existence of a family with all the stated fixed constants and guarantees, or prove its logical negation. A negative result must exclude every choice of positive constant rate, positive constant error tolerance and logarithmic-query constant for unbounded message lengths. A construction over a growing alphabet or a decoder that may fail on some requested positions under the allowed corruption guarantee does not establish the proposition.

context_blocks.title: Recover one item without reading everything
context_blocks.text: A file can be protected by adding redundant bits, yet reading the whole encoded file to retrieve one bit defeats the purpose of local access. Constant rate limits the storage overhead to one fixed factor. Constant error tolerance requires recovery even when a fixed positive fraction of the stored bits have been changed adversarially.

context_blocks.title: Why simple repetition does not suffice
context_blocks.text: Repeating every message bit three times gives constant rate and a three-query majority decoder. However, an adversary can spend just three corruptions on the requested bit’s copies. For large files this fits within any fixed positive global error budget and makes those copies look like a different message. Local redundancy alone therefore does not supply the guarantee for every requested position.

context_blocks.title: The remaining query gap
context_blocks.text: The April 2026 source records a logarithmic lower bound at constant rate, while the known binary high-rate construction uses \(2^{O(\sqrt{\log  n\cdot \log  \log  n})}\) queries. A bound of this latter form is subpolynomial but still larger than logarithmic. Its large-alphabet construction reaches polylogarithmic symbol queries; one such symbol can contain many bits, so it does not give the binary result here.

context_blocks.title: Related decoding guarantees
context_blocks.text: The January 2026 HDX paper gives approximate local list decoding and low-depth list decoding. A list may contain several plausible messages, and circuit depth measures parallel stages rather than bits inspected. Those results do not supply the single requested message bit with this card’s worst-case query and success guarantees.
